summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and coronary artery disease was admitted for acute shortness of breath. The symptom was attributed to fluid overload, likely due to interruption of his home diuretic (torsemide) after a recent gout admission and the salt-retaining effects of a prednisone taper. Initial concern for pulmonary embolism or heart failure was mitigated by a normal troponin, non-diagnostic D-dimer, and chest X-ray showing only minimal pulmonary vascular congestion. Renal function was stable relative to baseline, with a creatinine of 2.4 on admission improving to 2.1 at discharge. The transplant kidney ultrasound was stable with a new benign-appearing cyst. He responded well to IV furosemide and was discharged on his prior diuretic regimen with instructions to follow up in primary care and nephrology.
